title: The 'attention equation': Winning the right battles for consumer attention
summary: The media industry has historically measured success by quantity of consumer attention (hours watched, audience size) rather than quality, missing the true drivers of attention value. McKinsey's research introduces an "attention equation" that defines valuable attention as a function of focus and intent, not merely time spent. This framework reveals why digital media generates disproportionately low revenue relative to consumption share compared to legacy formats like broadcast television and live events.
central_argument: Attention value is determined by focus and intent, not consumption time, and this distinction explains why digital media monetizes attention far less effectively than legacy formats despite capturing significant consumption share.
key_claims: Consumer attention is finite while content supply has grown exponentially (25,000 times more hours produced on YouTube annually than traditional TV and streaming combined)
Live sports generate $33 per hour of attention value while podcasts generate $0.05, a 660-fold difference
Digital media captures disproportionately high consumption share (e.g., social media accounts for 13% of consumption but only 4% of revenue)
Total daily media consumption per American is roughly 13 hours, driven by simultaneous multitasking across devices
Inflation-adjusted media revenue has remained relatively flat despite growth in digital consumption
Focus and intent are the missing components in how attention value is calculated and monetized
key_tensions: The article challenges the assumption that more consumption automatically translates to higher monetization potential
It complicates the notion that audience size alone determines content value in the modern fragmented media landscape
It pushes back on treating all hours of attention equivalently regardless of consumer focus or engagement quality
key_entities: McKinsey consumer survey (7,000 consumers worldwide, 3,000 US-based)
